name: Skincare 'skin cycling'

angle.text: Skin cycling is used to get retinoid and exfoliant benefits for tone and texture while giving the skin barrier recovery nights. It spread through TikTok skincare circles. The rotation follows dermatology convention, but the schedule itself has not been trialled.

summary: TikTok-famous four-night rotation of exfoliant, retinoid and two recovery nights; reasonable by derm convention but never trialled.
note: No clinical studies of the routine itself.
currentQuick:
Skin cycling rotates an exfoliant night, a retinoid night and two recovery nights. It was popularised by dermatologist Whitney Bowe and spread on TikTok.
No clinical studies test the routine; dermatologists quoted describe it as a sensible, adaptable framework.
How it works: Spacing out actives is meant to limit irritation and give the skin barrier time to recover.
Risks and caveats: Retinoid and exfoliant irritation is possible; retinoid use in pregnancy is advised against by the AAD.
deepLead:
Skin cycling is a rotating skincare routine that alternates nights of exfoliant and retinoid use with nights of recovery. According to Grokipedia, it was created by New York dermatologist Whitney Bowe, introduced in April 2021, and went viral on TikTok in 2022 .
The stated aim is to gain the benefits of active ingredients while limiting irritation and protecting the skin barrier. The same source reports that no published clinical studies have tested skin cycling specifically, and that some dermatologists describe it as a reasonable but not revolutionary framework . Grokipedia is AI-generated and may contain errors.

name: Oral antibiotics (doxycycline/minocycline)

angle.text: Users in acne circles take prescribed doxycycline or minocycline to calm inflammatory breakouts and reduce red, active lesions for clearer skin. Their use in acne is established in dermatology, with trials supporting it.

summary: Prescription tetracyclines for inflammatory acne; established in dermatology, with documented side effects and resistance concerns.
note: Pregnancy and tooth-development warnings; minocycline pigmentation and lupus-like reactions.
currentQuick:
Doxycycline and minocycline are oral antibiotics that dermatologists prescribe for inflammatory acne and rosacea. They are usually paired with topical treatments.
Forum users discuss them for stubborn acne, with some voicing gut-health concerns.
How it works: They inhibit bacterial protein synthesis and also have anti-inflammatory effects.
Risks and caveats: Doxycycline: GI upset, sun sensitivity, esophagitis. Minocycline: pigmentation, drug-induced lupus, dizziness, rare intracranial hypertension. Both are warned against in pregnancy and childhood tooth development. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Doxycycline and minocycline are tetracycline-class antibiotics that dermatologists prescribe for inflammatory acne and rosacea. Both are prescription-only in the US and other countries .
Wikipedia reports that doxycycline is used at higher doses for severe acne and rosacea and at lower subantimicrobial doses long term, with benefit thought to come partly from anti-inflammatory effects . Minocycline is approved for inflammatory lesions of moderate-to-severe acne in people aged nine and older, with oral courses typically three to four months and limited data beyond that . Because of antibiotic resistance, oral antibiotics are generally combined with topical acne treatments .

name: Topical clindamycin

angle.text: Prescribed clindamycin gel or lotion is used, usually alongside benzoyl peroxide, to reduce mild to moderate inflammatory breakouts and get clearer skin. Its use in acne is well studied in clinical trials.

summary: Rx antibiotic gel or lotion for mild to moderate acne, usually paired with benzoyl peroxide; well studied, with resistance a recognised concern.
note: Resistance concerns; usually combined with benzoyl peroxide.
currentQuick:
Topical clindamycin is a prescription antibiotic for mild to moderate acne. It is usually combined with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid.
Wikipedia reports the combination works better than clindamycin alone.
How it works: It blocks bacterial protein synthesis; combinations aim to counter resistant bacteria.
Risks and caveats: Dryness, burning, itching, peeling and contact dermatitis are reported in over 10% of users. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Topical clindamycin is a prescription antibiotic lotion, gel or foam used for mild to moderate acne, often combined with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid. It is a semisynthetic derivative of lincomycin, announced in 1966 and marketed since 1968 .
Wikipedia reports that adding benzoyl peroxide to clindamycin works better than clindamycin alone . Randomised trials from the 1990s and 2000s compared clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide gels with each component and vehicle . Topical use commonly causes dryness, burning or peeling in over 10% of users .

name: Dapsone gel (Aczone)

angle.text: Dapsone gel is a prescription topical that acne forum posters use to calm inflamed breakouts, often as an alternative when other topicals irritate. Large phase 3 trials have studied it specifically for acne.

summary: Rx anti-inflammatory gel for acne with large phase 3 trial programs; usually mild irritation.
note: Can discolor skin when used with benzoyl peroxide.
currentQuick:
Dapsone gel (Aczone) is a prescription topical for acne. It has been studied in large registered trials, including in children and people with skin of color.
It is available in 5% and 7.5% strengths.
How it works: Dapsone inhibits bacterial folate synthesis and has anti-inflammatory activity through myeloperoxidase inhibition.
Risks and caveats: Mild irritation, dryness, redness; temporary yellow-orange discoloration with benzoyl peroxide. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Dapsone gel, sold as Aczone, is a prescription topical gel for acne vulgaris. Wikipedia reports that QLT USA developed the 5% gel in the early 2000s and that the FDA approved a 7.5% gel in February 2016 .
Dapsone has both antibacterial and anti-inflammatory actions, and Wikipedia reports that the 5% gel did not cause clinically significant hemoglobin declines in people with G6PD deficiency . Many registered trials have studied the gel, including two phase 3 studies enrolling over 2,000 patients each .

name: Sarecycline (Seysara)

angle.text: Sarecycline is a once-daily prescription tetracycline that people with moderate to severe inflammatory acne take to clear facial and body breakouts. It was approved for that use in 2018 and has been studied in acne trials.

summary: A once-daily, narrow-spectrum oral tetracycline approved in 2018 for inflammatory acne; a prescription antibiotic, not a looksmaxxing staple.
note: Prescription-only antibiotic; labelled for inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne, ages 9 and up.
currentQuick:
Sarecycline (brand name Seysara) is an oral antibiotic in the tetracycline class. The US FDA approved it in October 2018 for the inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne vulgaris in patients aged 9 and older [1][2].
It is taken once daily by prescription and was developed to act mainly against the skin bacterium Cutibacterium acnes while sparing much of the gut flora, a profile that differs from older tetracyclines such as doxycycline and minocycline [3].
How it works: Like other tetracyclines, sarecycline blocks bacterial protein synthesis. Its distinctive chemical side chain contacts bacterial messenger RNA, and reference sources describe a narrow spectrum aimed at Gram-positive skin bacteria with little activity against common Gram-negative gut bacteria [3].
Risks and caveats: As a tetracycline-class antibiotic it is prescription-only and is used under medical supervision. Guidelines for acne antibiotics in general advise limiting oral courses to about three months because of antibiotic resistance concerns [4]. Safety data from the pivotal trials are summarised in published reviews [2].
deepLead:
Sarecycline, sold in the United States under the brand name Seysara, is an oral tetracycline-class antibiotic approved for acne vulgaris. The FDA approved the tablet formulation in early October 2018 for the treatment of inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne in patients aged 9 years and older .
It was developed by Paratek and Allergan and later acquired by the dermatology-focused company Almirall . It is described as a narrow-spectrum tetracycline, meaning that it is aimed mainly at Cutibacterium acnes and has little activity against the Gram-negative bacteria typical of the human gut .
Sarecycline is a conventional prescription acne medicine rather than a product that originated in looksmaxxing culture. The sources reviewed for this article contain no substantial forum discussion of it. Its inclusion in the wiki reflects its place among oral options for acne, a common concern in skin-focused appearance discussions.

name: Combined oral contraceptive pill

angle.text: Women use the combined pill, prescribed off its main contraceptive purpose, to reduce hormonal acne by lowering androgen activity and sebum. Its use for acne is studied and recognised in dermatology.

summary: The estrogen-plus-progestin birth control pill, also prescribed for hormonal acne in women because it lowers free androgens.
note: Prescription-only; carries a small increased venous clotting risk and has formal contraindications.
currentQuick:
Combined oral contraceptives contain an estrogen and a progestin. Besides preventing pregnancy, some are prescribed to reduce acne and excess hair growth in women, because they lower the activity of androgen hormones that drive oil production in skin [1][2].
Wikipedia reports that four combined pills are FDA-approved for moderate acne in people who have started menstruating and also want contraception, and that studies show reductions in both inflammatory and non-inflammatory facial lesions [1]. Progestin-only pills have not been shown to help acne [1].
How it works: The estrogen component appears to suppress ovarian androgen production and raises sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), which reduces free testosterone. Lower free androgens mean less sebum, a major contributor to acne [1].
Risks and caveats: Common effects include breakthrough bleeding, nausea, headache, breast tenderness and bloating. Venous thromboembolism risk is higher in users than non-users in absolute terms (about 60 versus 30 per 100,000 woman-years) and varies by progestin; the FDA added a warning to drospirenone pill labels in 2012. Smoking over 35, migraine with aura, and a history of clots or stroke are among the listed contraindications [1].
deepLead:
The combined oral contraceptive pill (COC) is a hormonal medicine containing an estrogen and a progestin, taken mainly for contraception. It is also prescribed for acne and hirsutism in women, since lowering androgen activity reduces sebum production .
Four combined pills are FDA-approved for moderate acne in patients who are at least 14 or 15 years old, have begun menstruating, and need contraception: Ortho Tri-Cyclen, Estrostep, Beyaz and YAZ . Wikipedia's acne article reports lesion reductions of roughly 40 to 70 percent with combined pills, and notes that a 2014 review found oral antibiotics somewhat better at three months but roughly equal at six months .
The pill is a conventional prescription treatment. In looksmaxxing and skin-care communities it is relevant mainly to women's discussions of hormonal acne; the sources reviewed for this article contain no substantial forum material about it.

name: Low-dose isotretinoin (microdosing Accutane)

chain: Clear skin with fewer side effects
angle.text: Forum posters discuss taking small continuous isotretinoin amounts instead of a full course to keep acne away with milder side effects, sometimes as maintenance after a course. Low-dose regimens have been studied in acne, but online protocols are mostly anecdotal.

summary: Using small continuous isotretinoin (Accutane) amounts, instead of a standard course, to keep acne away with fewer side effects; discussed online, thinly documented here.
note: Isotretinoin is a prescription teratogen with a boxed psychiatric warning; regimens are set by a prescriber.
currentQuick:
Low-dose isotretinoin, often called microdosing Accutane online, refers to taking much smaller amounts of the prescription acne drug than a standard course, sometimes continuously, with the stated aim of keeping skin clear while reducing side effects.
On looksmax.org, users discuss whether a small maintenance amount after a full course could help results last, and some combine the idea with a topical retinoid [1]. The reference sources reviewed for this article describe isotretinoin's standard use and risks but give no low-dose study results [2].
How it works: Isotretinoin is described as the only acne drug affecting all four main processes in acne [2]. The rationale given by proponents is that a smaller exposure might preserve benefit with fewer dose-related effects; the sources reviewed here do not test that idea.
Risks and caveats: Isotretinoin is prescription-only in most countries, a known teratogen (US Pregnancy Category X) and subject to the iPLEDGE programme in the US. Common effects include dry lips, skin and eyes; psychiatric effects have been reported and the US label has carried a boxed warning since 2005 [2].
deepLead:
Low-dose isotretinoin, popularly called microdosing Accutane, is the practice of taking markedly smaller doses of isotretinoin than the standard acne regimen, in some cases as an ongoing maintenance approach. Isotretinoin is a prescription retinoid first patented by Roche in 1969 and approved by the FDA in 1982 .
Within looksmaxxing forums the idea appears as a way to preserve clear skin after a conventional course finishes. A looksmax.org thread, for instance, asks whether a small maintenance amount after finishing a cycle would help acne stay away, and a respondent says it would, adding that a low-strength topical retinoid is sometimes paired with it . These are individual user statements, not clinical findings.
The reference sources reviewed for this article do not report results for low-dose regimens. They do state that the dose may be lowered to reduce side effects and that psychiatric side-effect risk rises with dose . The entry is therefore documented mainly as a community practice.

name: Spearmint tea

angle.text: Spearmint tea is drunk by people with hormonal acne who hope it lowers androgens and clears breakouts. One small trial looked at androgen levels in PCOS; acne itself has not been tested.

summary: A herbal tea said to lower androgens and calm hormonal acne; one small trial studied androgens in PCOS, and none tested acne.
note: The human research is on androgens and hirsutism in PCOS, not on acne.
currentQuick:
Spearmint tea is an infusion of the leaves of Mentha spicata, a common culinary herb [1]. In skin-care and hormonal-acne circles it is promoted as a mild anti-androgen drink that could reduce oil and breakouts.
The human research behind the idea is a small randomized trial in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and excess hair growth, which examined anti-androgen effects [2]. A review of plant-derived anti-androgens discusses acne as one condition where such agents are of interest [3]. No trial in the sources reviewed tests spearmint tea on acne.
How it works: Proponents say compounds in spearmint lower circulating androgens such as testosterone, which drive sebum production. The PCOS trial title reports significant anti-androgen effects from the tea [2]; how this works and whether it reaches skin is not established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Spearmint is a common food flavouring and tea ingredient [1]. The sources reviewed contain no safety data specific to regular medicinal use of the tea.
deepLead:
Spearmint tea is made by steeping the leaves of spearmint (Mentha spicata), a perennial herb native to Europe and southern temperate Asia that is widely used as a flavouring and in teas such as Maghrebi mint tea .
In wellness and skin-care communities it is promoted as an anti-androgen drink for hormonal acne and for hirsutism. The research most often cited is a randomized controlled trial of spearmint herbal tea in women with PCOS, reported in 2010 in Phytotherapy Research, whose title states significant anti-androgen effects . That paper itself notes that it set out to test whether lowering androgens translates to clinical improvement in hirsutism, a question earlier work had not addressed .
A 2012 review of plant-derived anti-androgens lists acne alongside PCOS, hirsutism and prostate conditions as areas where reducing androgen activity matters, and discusses the growing recognition of plant-based options . No human trial in the sources reviewed tests spearmint tea for acne.

name: Low-glycemic diet for acne

angle.text: People with acne adopt a low-glycemic diet hoping that steadier blood sugar will reduce breakouts and give clearer skin. It is among the few diet changes with some trial support for acne, though the evidence is modest.

summary: Eating low-GI carbs to calm acne: the one diet tweak with some trial support, though the evidence is modest.
note: Glycemic index values vary with ripeness, cooking and the individual, and diet is not a substitute for medical acne care.
currentQuick:
A low-glycemic diet swaps fast-digesting carbohydrates such as white bread, sugary drinks and sweets for slower ones such as legumes, whole grains and most vegetables. In looksmaxxing and skincare circles it is discussed as a way to reduce acne without drugs.
According to Wikipedia's acne article, several randomized and non-randomized studies have reported that lower-glycemic-load diets reduced acne severity, and dermatologists commonly suggest a diet low in simple sugars. The overall body of evidence is described as emerging rather than settled.
How it works: The proposed mechanism is that high-glycemic meals raise blood glucose and insulin, which is thought to increase IGF-1 and androgen activity, and in turn sebum production and comedone formation. Androgens and IGF-1 are both considered important in acne biology.
Risks and caveats: A low-GI eating pattern is generally an ordinary dietary approach with no specific safety concerns identified in the sources. Glycemic index is an imperfect measure: some foods with a low GI are high in fat or sugar, and values vary between individuals and preparations.
deepLead:
A low-glycemic diet (low-GI or low-glycemic-load diet) is an eating pattern built around foods that raise blood glucose slowly, used by some people with acne in the hope of reducing breakouts. The glycemic index, introduced by David Jenkins and colleagues in 1981, ranks carbohydrate foods from 0 to 100 against pure glucose, and glycemic load adjusts that ranking for portion size.
Wikipedia's acne article reports that multiple randomized controlled trials and non-randomized studies found a lower-glycemic-load diet effective in reducing acne, and that dermatologists recommend a diet low in simple sugars. The same article describes the evidence for diet and acne as emerging, and says a causal relationship between diet and skin conditions is rarely observed.
Glycemic index itself has recognized limitations: values depend on ripeness, cooking and processing, individual responses differ, and some foods with a low GI are otherwise energy-dense.

name: Fungal acne protocol (Malassezia)

angle.text: People with stubborn, itchy forehead or body bumps avoid fatty-acid oils and use antifungal washes aiming to clear them. Malassezia folliculitis is a recognised condition treated with antifungals, though self-diagnosis in forums is common.

summary: Avoiding fatty-acid oils and using antifungals for itchy forehead and body bumps attributed to Malassezia yeast, a recognised condition called Malassezia folliculitis.
note: The condition is recognised in dermatology; the specific product-avoidance rules circulating online are not tested in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Fungal acne is the popular name for Malassezia (formerly Pityrosporum) folliculitis, in which yeast that normally lives on skin overgrows in hair follicles and causes itchy, uniform pustules, most often on the upper trunk and sometimes the forehead [1][2]. Online, the term also covers a skincare protocol: avoiding products with certain oils and fatty acids and using antifungal treatments.
Looksmax.org threads show users reporting forehead bumps and flaking that they attribute to fungal acne or seborrheic dermatitis and asking which products to use, with some saying ordinary acne approaches did not help [3][4].
How it works: Malassezia are lipophilic yeasts that need fatty acids to grow; Wikipedia reports they consume fatty acids with chains of about 11 to 24 carbons [1]. This is the basis for the avoid-certain-oils idea. Research has linked resident Malassezia species to the folliculitis [5].
Risks and caveats: Malassezia are part of normal skin flora and are linked to several skin conditions including seborrheic dermatitis [6]. Diagnosis is clinical and by distribution [1]; Danish treatment guidelines exist for Malassezia-related disease [7]. Persistent bumps are generally assessed by a dermatologist.
deepLead:
Fungal acne is a popular name for Malassezia folliculitis, also called pityrosporum folliculitis. It is a skin condition in which yeast of the genus Malassezia, a normal part of human skin flora, overgrows within hair follicles and produces itchy papules and pustules . Despite the name it is not acne vulgaris, which involves different processes.
Wikipedia describes it as occurring most often on the upper trunk (back, chest, arms) in young to middle-aged adults, with overgrowth associated with oily skin, humidity and conditions such as seborrheic dermatitis or severe dandruff . Malassezia are lipophilic, depending on fatty acids found in skin oils to multiply .
In looksmaxxing and skincare forums, the phrase also names a protocol: avoiding fatty-acid-containing oils and ingredients in products and using antifungal treatments. Looksmax.org threads show users describing forehead bumps and flaking, sometimes alongside seborrheic dermatitis, and asking what to use . The sources reviewed do not trial the protocol as a whole.

name: Double cleansing

angle.text: Skincare communities use an oil cleanser followed by a foaming cleanser in the evening to fully remove sunscreen, makeup and oil for clearer skin. The routine comes from Korean and Japanese beauty practice and has not been trialled.

summary: Oil cleanser first, foam cleanser second; a popular nightly routine that no trial has actually tested.
note: Evidence is limited to general cleansing guidance; some first-step oils are described as pore-clogging for some people.
currentQuick:
Double cleansing means washing the face twice in the evening: first with an oil, balm or micellar water, then with a water-based cleanser. It comes from Korean and Japanese beauty routines.
Proponents say it removes sunscreen, makeup and sebum more completely than a single wash. No published trial has tested the routine itself.
How it works: The oil step dissolves oil-soluble residues such as sunscreen and sebum; the water-based step then removes what remains and rinses the oil away.
Risks and caveats: Risks are mild and mainly relate to irritation from over-washing and, for some people, breakouts from comedogenic oils. Evidence for cleansing practices in general is described as limited.
deepLead:
Double cleansing is a two-step facial washing routine in which an oil-based or other lipid-soluble cleanser (a cleansing oil, balm or micellar water) is applied first, followed by a water-based cleanser that is emulsified with water and rinsed off. It is associated with Korean and Japanese beauty routines and is described in looksmaxxing and skincare communities as an evening step used to remove sunscreen, makeup and sebum.
Proponents say the first step dissolves oil-soluble residues such as water-resistant sunscreen and waterproof makeup that a single water-based wash may leave behind, and that the second step removes the remaining oil and water-soluble debris. Dermatologists quoted in general references describe cleansing as a routine part of acne care but note that evidence for specific cleansing practices is limited. No published clinical trial has tested double cleansing as a regimen for acne or appearance.

name: Skin cycling

angle.text: Skin cycling is used for acne, scars, fine lines and glow by rotating acid and retinoid nights with recovery nights, and is promoted for sensitive or acne-prone skin. It was popularised by a dermatologist and TikTok; the schedule itself has not been trialled.

summary: A four-night rotation of acid, retinoid and two rest nights; popular and plausible, but the schedule itself has never been trialled.
note: Retinoids and exfoliants increase sun sensitivity; daily sunscreen is part of the method.
currentQuick:
Skin cycling rotates a four-night routine: an exfoliating acid, then a retinoid, then two nights with no actives. It was introduced by dermatologist Whitney Bowe in 2021 and went viral on TikTok.
Supporters say it cuts irritation while still using strong ingredients. No clinical study has tested the schedule itself.
How it works: The idea is that rest nights let the skin barrier recover between exfoliation and retinoid use, so irritation builds less than with daily actives.
Risks and caveats: Exfoliants and retinoids can cause dryness, redness and sun sensitivity, so sunscreen is part of the routine. It is not described as a replacement for professional treatment of severe acne.
deepLead:
Skin cycling is a skincare routine that rotates evenings of active ingredients with evenings of recovery. It was introduced in April 2021 by New York dermatologist Whitney Bowe and spread widely on TikTok in 2022.
The standard four-night cycle uses a chemical exfoliant on night one, a retinoid on night two, and no actives on nights three and four, when moisturising and barrier-supporting products are used instead. Mornings are the same each day: gentle cleansing and broad-spectrum sunscreen. Proponents say it reduces irritation while building tolerance to retinoids and exfoliants.
No published clinical studies have tested this specific schedule. Dermatologists quoted in general references describe it as a reasonable framework consistent with alternating strong actives with rest, while noting that retinoid data mostly support regular use.

name: Oil cleansing method

angle.text: Users massage plant oils into the face to dissolve sebum, makeup and sunscreen, aiming for clearer, brighter skin and sometimes fewer breakouts. It is popular and debated in acne circles, and the method itself has not been trialled.

summary: Massage oil in to dissolve sebum and makeup; popular and divisive for acne, with no trials of the method itself.
note: Comedogenic oils such as coconut oil may clog pores; irritation reported in acne- or rosacea-prone skin.
currentQuick:
The oil cleansing method uses a plant oil massaged into dry skin to dissolve makeup, sunscreen and sebum, followed by rinsing. It grew out of online forums in the mid-2000s and later merged with Korean double cleansing.
Supporters say it cleans without stripping skin. Dermatologist guidance is cautious for acne-prone skin, and the method itself is not well studied.
How it works: Oils dissolve oil-soluble substances such as sebum, sunscreen and makeup, and are then emulsified with water and rinsed away.
Risks and caveats: Comedogenic oils may cause breakouts, and additives such as essential oils can cause allergic or irritant reactions, especially in acne-prone or rosacea-prone skin.
deepLead:
The oil cleansing method is a facial cleansing practice in which a plant oil, or blend of oils, is massaged into dry skin to dissolve makeup, sunscreen and sebum, then emulsified with water and rinsed or wiped off. Common blends pair a thicker oil such as castor oil with a lighter carrier oil, and it is frequently used as the first step of a double cleanse.
Proponents say it removes oil-based debris without stripping the skin's natural lipids and can improve hydration and help manage acne. Dermatologist guidance summarised in reference sources is cautious: it may suit dry or mature skin but may cause breakouts or irritation, especially in acne-prone or rosacea-prone skin. Research on the method itself is limited.

name: Chemical peels for acne

angle.text: Salicylic, glycolic and Jessner peels are used in clinics and at home to clear acne, reduce oil, and fade marks and scars. Small studies exist for acne, while guidelines describe the evidence as insufficient.

summary: Salicylic, glycolic or Jessner peels for acne; small studies exist, but guidance calls evidence insufficient to recommend them.
note: Redness, pigment change and scarring are possible, including with home kits.
currentQuick:
Chemical peels apply acids such as salicylic, glycolic or TCA to remove the top skin layers, and are used for acne and acne marks in clinics or, at lower strengths, at home.
Salicylic acid is the agent most associated with acne. Small studies exist, but a general skincare reference says evidence is insufficient to recommend peels for acne.
How it works: The acid causes a controlled injury that sheds the outer skin layers. Salicylic acid is oil-soluble, and is described as antibacterial and anti-inflammatory.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include redness, photosensitivity, pigment changes, milia and scarring, including from low-strength home kits. Concern about pigment complications has limited medium-depth peel use in darker skin.
deepLead:
A chemical peel is a treatment, most often applied to the face, in which a chemical agent removes the outer skin layers; the controlled injury causes peeling and can smooth texture and reduce acne scars and pigmentation. For acne, the agents most often discussed are salicylic acid (a beta hydroxy acid), glycolic acid (an alpha hydroxy acid), Jessner solution and trichloroacetic acid (TCA), used in a dermatology office or, at lower strengths, at home.
Salicylic acid is oil-soluble, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory, and is described as increasingly preferred over alpha hydroxy acids for acne. Small clinical studies have compared peels for acne, but a general skincare reference states that evidence is insufficient to recommend chemical peels for acne, although dermatologists sometimes use them alongside medical treatment.

name: Photodynamic therapy (ALA-PDT)

chain: Light activates photosensitizer in oil glands
angle.text: People with severe or stubborn acne pursue ALA-PDT in clinics to target oil glands and inflamed lesions, sometimes on the body too. Some trials and a review report benefit for acne, with mixed results.

summary: Photosensitizer plus light for severe acne; some trials and a review are positive, but results are mixed and treatment is painful.
note: Clinician-administered; pain, redness and photosensitivity are common.
currentQuick:
ALA-PDT applies aminolevulinic acid to the skin and then light, which kills targeted cells. It is established for actinic keratosis and some skin cancers and has been studied for severe acne.
A 2016 review called it safe and effective for acne, while one phase II trial found no advantage over blue or violet light alone.
How it works: ALA makes cells accumulate protoporphyrin IX, which on light exposure produces reactive oxygen species that damage the treated cells.
Risks and caveats: Marked redness, moderate to severe pain, burning and photosensitivity are reported. It is performed by clinicians.
deepLead:
Photodynamic therapy (PDT) uses a light-sensitive drug (photosensitizer) and light of a suitable wavelength to produce reactive oxygen species that kill targeted cells. In ALA-PDT, aminolevulinic acid (ALA), a precursor in the body's heme synthesis, is applied so that cells accumulate the photosensitizer protoporphyrin IX before light is shone on the area.
Dermatologically it is best established for actinic keratosis and certain skin cancers. For acne it has been studied mainly in severe or inflammatory acne. A 2016 systematic review described it as safe and effective for acne, while one phase II trial found it no better than blue or violet light alone, according to a general reference. Reported side effects in acne treatment include marked redness, moderate to severe pain and burning.

name: Professional extractions / acne facial

chain: Manual removal of blackheads and whiteheads
angle.text: An esthetician or dermatologist manually clears blackheads and whiteheads, giving visibly cleaner pores right after the session. It is standard acne facial practice, with little formal trial evidence on long-term outcomes.

summary: Manual blackhead and whitehead removal by a pro; standard practice, with little formal trial evidence.
note: Poorly done extraction can cause infection or scarring.
currentQuick:
Professional extraction is manual removal of blackheads and whiteheads by an esthetician or dermatologist, often during an acne facial.
Open comedones are generally easier to remove than closed ones. Sources found no controlled trials specific to the practice.
How it works: A comedo extractor applies pressure to expel the keratin and oil plug, usually after steaming or warm washing.
Risks and caveats: Picking or squeezing risks infection and scarring; hygiene and technique matter, and dermabrasion or laser can also scar.
deepLead:
Professional comedone extraction is the manual removal of blackheads and whiteheads by an esthetician or dermatologist, usually as part of an acne facial. Practitioners use comedo extractors with attention to hygiene, typically after steaming the face or washing with warm water.
A comedo is a hair follicle clogged with keratin and oil; it is open (a blackhead, dark from oxidation rather than dirt) or closed (a whitehead). Dermatologists can often remove open comedones with minimal skin trauma, while closed comedones are harder to remove. No controlled trial specific to esthetician extractions appears in the available sources.

name: Intralesional cortisone injection

chain: Swelling drops within a day or two
angle.text: People with a large painful cyst before an event get a clinician to inject cortisone, commonly described as shrinking it overnight. The visible flattening is widely reported in appearance communities; trial detail was not covered in the sources reviewed.

summary: A dermatologist-administered steroid shot into an inflamed cyst, discussed online as an overnight shrinker; evidence is not detailed in the sources reviewed.
note: Clinician-administered procedure; reported to be able to affect the skin locally and glucocorticoids can worsen acne.
currentQuick:
An intralesional cortisone injection is a clinic procedure where a corticosteroid is injected straight into an inflamed acne cyst or nodule. People in looksmaxxing and skincare circles discuss it as a fast way to reduce a large lesion.
Wikipedia describes it as providing immediate relief for inflamed acne lesions.
How it works: The corticosteroid is delivered into the lesion, where its anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid action is directed at the inflamed tissue.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed give little detail on side effects. Glucocorticoids are noted to be able to worsen acne in general, and the procedure is performed by clinicians.
deepLead:
An intralesional cortisone injection is a procedure in which a clinician injects a corticosteroid directly into an inflamed lesion, such as a painful acne cyst or nodule. In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a way to flatten a large pimple quickly, often described as shrinking a cyst "overnight".
Wikipedia lists injection of a corticosteroid into an inflamed acne lesion among the procedures used for acne, describing it as offering rapid relief . Triamcinolone acetonide, a synthetic glucocorticoid, is one corticosteroid injected into skin lesions such as keloids and hypertrophic scars .

name: Toothpaste on pimples

Dabbing toothpaste on a pimple overnight is a long-circulating home remedy for acne. Practitioners say it dries out the spot.
Toothpaste is formulated for teeth: it typically contains abrasives, fluoride, surfactants such as sodium lauryl sulfate, flavourings and sometimes antibacterial agents . Wikipedia's toothpaste article does not discuss use on acne, and its acne article does not list toothpaste among treatments .

name: Apple cider vinegar toner

angle.text: Home-remedy fans apply diluted apple cider vinegar as a toner for acne and oily skin. The idea rests on its acidity and anecdotes, and no studies were found on its use for acne.

summary: Diluted ACV dabbed on the face as an acne toner; no studies found and burns are documented.

currentQuick:
People mix apple cider vinegar with water and apply it to the face as a toner, aiming at acne and oil.
No clinical studies on this use were found; Wikipedia describes evidence for skin conditions as poor.
How it works: ACV contains about 5% acetic acid, an acid that proponents believe balances or clears skin; this is not established in studies.
Risks and caveats: Burns from topical vinegar and eye injury on contact are documented; acidity varies between brands.
deepLead:
Apple cider vinegar (ACV) toner is a diluted vinegar applied to the face as a homemade toner, which proponents use for acne and oiliness.
ACV is made by fermenting apple juice into acetic acid and is about 5% acetic acid . Wikipedia states that evidence for treating skin infections with it is poor and that applying vinegar to skin conditions may cause burns . Major health organisations do not recommend it as a therapy .

name: Lemon juice on pimples

Some people apply lemon juice to pimples, citing its citric acid and vitamin C.

deepLead:
Dabbing lemon juice on pimples is a home remedy for acne and dark marks. Proponents cite its acidity and vitamin C.
